outline.description: This chapter introduces the central problem the paper addresses: modern language models depend on fixed-vocabulary tokenization, even though tokenization is a hand-designed preprocessing step with important weaknesses. It motivates byte-level modeling, explains why it has historically been too expensive, and presents the Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) as a way to recover both performance and efficiency.

outline.chapter_title: Foundations: Bytes, Tokens, Patches, and Compute
outline.description: Before studying BLT, readers need a clear vocabulary for the units of language modeling and the metrics used to compare systems. This chapter builds the conceptual foundation for understanding bytes, subword tokens, patches, autoregressive modeling, FLOPs, and bits-per-byte.

outline.chapter_title: From Bytes to Patches: The Patching Problem
outline.description: BLT replaces tokens with dynamically formed patches, so the design of the patching function becomes central. This chapter formalizes patching and compares the main alternatives explored in the paper, including why some methods are easy to implement but poorly matched to the true complexity of language.
subtopics: Formal definition of a patching function

outline.chapter_title: Entropy Patching: Learning Where Compute Should Go
outline.description: This chapter explains BLT's key innovation for dynamic segmentation: using the entropy of next-byte predictions to decide where new patches should begin. It develops the intuition that difficult, high-uncertainty regions deserve more global computation, while predictable regions can be grouped into longer patches.
subtopics: Why entropy is a useful proxy for local prediction difficulty

outline.chapter_title: BLT at a High Level: A Hierarchical Byte-Level Language Model
outline.description: BLT is not just a new patching rule; it is a new architecture built around patches as latent units of computation. This chapter gives the full system view: a lightweight byte-level encoder, a large global Transformer that operates on patch representations, and a lightweight byte-level decoder that predicts raw bytes.
subtopics: The three-part BLT architecture: encoder, global model, decoder

outline.chapter_title: The Local Encoder: Turning Byte Sequences into Patch Representations
outline.description: This chapter dives into the encoder, whose job is to build expressive latent patch embeddings from raw bytes at low cost. It explains the encoder's byte embeddings, hash n-gram augmentation, local attention, and patch-restricted cross-attention pooling.

outline.chapter_title: The Global Transformer and Local Decoder
outline.description: After the encoder creates patch representations, BLT uses a large autoregressive latent Transformer to model patch-level dependencies and a lightweight decoder to convert those latent predictions back into bytes. This chapter explains both modules and how they cooperate during training and inference.

outline.chapter_title: Training BLT Fairly: Data, Hyperparameters, and Measurement
outline.description: To compare BLT against token-based LLMs, the paper carefully controls for data, context, and compute. This chapter walks through the experimental design so readers can understand why the reported comparisons are meaningful.

outline.chapter_title: Compute-Optimal Scaling: Matching Token-Based LLMs at Scale
outline.description: This chapter presents the paper's central scaling result: BLT is the first byte-level Transformer architecture shown to match tokenization-based LLM performance in a FLOP-controlled setting at large scale. It explains the experiments, the comparisons, and the importance of combining architecture changes with dynamic patching.

outline.description: The paper argues that BLT opens a new scaling dimension unavailable to token-based models: one can increase both model size and patch size while holding inference cost fixed. outline.chapter_title: Robustness, Character Knowledge, and the Long Tail of Language
outline.description: A major advantage of direct byte modeling is that the model retains access to fine-grained text structure that token-based systems often blur away. This chapter examines the paper's robustness and character-level evaluations, showing where byte-level modeling yields large practical gains.
